title: Given a Scenario, Use the Appropriate Cloud Service Model

sections.title: What You Are Learning
paragraphs: Cloud service models answer one major question: How much of the technology stack does the cloud provider manage, and how much remains your responsibility?

CompTIA may describe an organization that wants more control, less administration, a ready-to-use application, or the ability to run small pieces of code without managing servers. Your job is to recognize which service model best matches that requirement.
The four models in this objective are Infrastructure as a service (IaaS), Platform as a service (PaaS), Software as a service (SaaS), and Function as a service (FaaS).
The biggest difference between them is how much responsibility moves from the customer to the cloud provider.

sections.title: Maestro Focus
paragraphs: How much of the environment does the organization want to manage itself?
sections.callout: More customer control → think IaaS. More provider management → move toward PaaS, SaaS, or FaaS depending on the workload.

sections.title: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
paragraphs: IaaS provides the basic computing infrastructure needed to build an environment.
The cloud provider supplies resources such as computing, storage, and networking, while the customer maintains significant control over what happens inside the environment.
The customer may still configure and maintain operating systems, applications, software configuration, and workload settings.
Think: The cloud provider gives me the building materials, but I still build and maintain much of the house.
IaaS is useful when an organization wants cloud flexibility but still needs control over its systems.

entries.title: Example
paragraphs: A company wants to move several existing servers into the cloud while continuing to manage the operating systems and applications. That points toward IaaS.
entries.recognitionCue: If you see virtual infrastructure with customer-managed operating systems → think IaaS.

sections.title: Platform as a Service (PaaS)
paragraphs: PaaS gives developers a managed environment where they can build and deploy applications without managing as much of the underlying infrastructure.
Instead of spending time maintaining the operating system and supporting platform, developers can concentrate more heavily on the application itself.
Think: Give me the workshop so I can build the application.
PaaS is especially useful when the focus is application development, application deployment, and reduced operating-system administration.

entries.title: Example
paragraphs: A development team wants to deploy a web application but does not want to maintain the servers or operating system running underneath it. That points toward PaaS.
entries.recognitionCue: If developers need a managed environment for building or deploying applications → think PaaS.

sections.title: Software as a Service (SaaS)
paragraphs: SaaS provides a finished application that users access as a service.
The customer is primarily concerned with using the software, not building or maintaining the infrastructure behind it.
The provider manages the application and the underlying platform and infrastructure.
Think: I just want to use the software.
Common SaaS scenarios involve organizations wanting a ready-to-use application without maintaining the servers supporting that application.

entries.title: Example
paragraphs: A business wants employees to use an online application without installing and maintaining its own application servers. That points toward SaaS.
entries.recognitionCue: If the customer simply needs to use a completed cloud-hosted application → think SaaS.

sections.title: Function as a Service (FaaS)
paragraphs: FaaS allows developers to execute individual pieces of code in response to an event or request without managing the servers that run that code.
The developer provides the function. The cloud environment handles the infrastructure needed to execute it.
Think: Run this piece of code when something happens.
FaaS can be useful when code needs to run only when triggered instead of requiring a continuously managed server environment.

entries.title: Example
paragraphs: An application needs a small piece of code to run automatically whenever a user uploads a file. The developer wants the code to execute when needed without maintaining a dedicated server. That points toward FaaS.
entries.recognitionCue: If event-driven code must run without managing servers → think FaaS.

sections.title: IaaS vs. PaaS vs. SaaS vs. FaaS
paragraphs: A useful mental progression is: IaaS → manage more; PaaS → build more, manage less; SaaS → use the software; FaaS → provide the function and let the platform execute it.

sections.title: Shared Responsibility Model
paragraphs: Moving something into the cloud does not mean the customer has zero security or management responsibility.
The shared responsibility model divides responsibility between the cloud provider and the cloud customer. Exactly where that dividing line sits depends heavily on the service model being used.
With IaaS, the customer generally has more responsibility because the customer manages more of the environment.
With SaaS, the provider manages much more of the underlying technology, but the customer still has responsibilities related to how the service is used.
Think: Cloud does not eliminate responsibility. It redistributes responsibility.

sections.title: The Service Model Connection
paragraphs: As you move from IaaS toward more fully managed services, customer management generally decreases and provider management generally increases.
That distinction is one of the easiest ways to identify the correct service model in a scenario.
bullets: If CompTIA asks who manages what → think shared responsibility model.
If the customer wants greater control → think toward IaaS.
If the customer wants the provider to manage more → think toward PaaS or SaaS depending on whether they are building or simply using software.

sections.title: Recognition Cues
bullets: Customer manages operating systems → IaaS
Need cloud infrastructure with significant customer control → IaaS
Developers want to build applications without managing the OS → PaaS
Need a managed application development environment → PaaS
Users simply need a finished application → SaaS
No desire to maintain the application platform → SaaS
Small event-driven code executes when triggered → FaaS
Run code without managing servers → FaaS
Question asks where customer responsibility ends and provider responsibility begins → Shared responsibility model

entries.title: PaaS vs. SaaS
paragraphs: Both reduce infrastructure management, but they solve different problems. PaaS is for building and deploying applications. SaaS is the finished application.
If the scenario describes developers creating software, lean toward PaaS. If the scenario describes employees simply using software, lean toward SaaS.

entries.title: PaaS vs. FaaS
paragraphs: Both allow developers to avoid managing much of the underlying infrastructure. The difference is what the developer is deploying.
PaaS → application environment. FaaS → individual function or piece of code that runs when triggered.

entries.title: Cloud vs. Zero Responsibility
paragraphs: Do not assume that moving to SaaS means the customer has no responsibilities.
The provider manages more of the technology, but the cloud environment still follows a shared responsibility model.
